name: Atomic Notes
description: Atomic notes are one idea per card—small enough to move, remix, and reuse. Think LEGO bricks for thinking: tiny pieces that snap into bigger structures without breaking. citeturn9search0

name: Evergreen Notes
description: Evergreen notes are notes you keep rewriting until they stay true as you learn. They’re like a living user manual for your brain: each edit makes it clearer, not longer. citeturn1search10

name: Fleeting Notes
description: Fleeting notes are quick scratchpads that catch an idea before it disappears. Their job is capture, not beauty—like jotting a phone number on your hand so you don’t lose it. citeturn11search8

name: Literature Notes
description: Literature notes are what the source said, in your own words, with a breadcrumb back to the source. They’re like copying a recipe before you start improvising. citeturn9search0

name: Permanent Notes
description: Permanent notes are your own claims written so they make sense tomorrow without extra context. It’s the difference between “I read something” and “Here’s the idea I stand behind.” citeturn9search0

name: Zettelkasten Slip-Box
description: A Zettelkasten is a box of linked slips where each slip is a thought and the links let thoughts talk. It’s like building a paper internet for your mind—small pages, many crossroads. citeturn9search0turn10search2

name: Kommunikation mit Zettelkästen
description: Luhmann described his slip-box as a conversation partner: you follow links, and the system surprises you back. The “magic” is just lots of linked thoughts plus a habit of revisiting them. citeturn11search2turn11search6

name: Unique ID Addressing
description: Unique IDs give every note a stable address so links don’t break when titles change. It’s like street numbers: you can repaint the house, but the address still works. citeturn10search2

name: Backlinks
description: Backlinks show “who points to me,” turning notes into neighborhoods instead of folders. When you see all incoming paths, you find hidden clusters and unexpected connections. citeturn1search10

name: Bidirectional Links
description: Bidirectional links mean if A links to B, B remembers A. That one feature turns notes into a web, like roads that appear on both the departure map and the arrival map. citeturn9search0

name: Graph Structure
description: Graph structure is the shape your links create—dense hubs, bridges, and dead ends. It’s like a city map of your mind: downtowns signal deep themes; empty roads signal neglected ideas. citeturn10search1

name: Map of Content (MOC)
description: A Map of Content is a hand-made trail map through your notes. Instead of searching from scratch every time, you build a few “main roads” that make exploration fast and calm. citeturn1search10

name: Index Note
description: An index note is a table of contents for a topic in your system. It lists the best entry points so you can jump back in without rereading the entire library. citeturn9search0

name: Progressive Summarization
description: Progressive summarization is rereading in layers: capture, then highlight the best, then write the “gold sentence.” It’s panning for gold—each pass removes more sand. citeturn11search12

name: Compression Ladder
description: A compression ladder is raw source → summary → your claim → your output. The goal is speed without amnesia: you can act fast while keeping the deep version available when needed. citeturn11search12

name: Capture Funnel
description: A capture funnel is one trusted doorway for ideas: everything lands somewhere safe first, then you sort later. It prevents the worst failure—an idea you never wrote down. citeturn11search8

name: Inbox Zero for Ideas
description: Inbox Zero for ideas means “nothing undecided,” not “nothing incoming.” You clear mental nagging by choosing: trash, keep, schedule, or incubate—then your brain can relax. citeturn11search8

name: Actionability Filter
description: An actionability filter asks: will this help me make, decide, or teach? If not, it’s often just attention candy. You’re building a workshop, not a junk museum. citeturn11search0turn8search6

name: PARA Method
description: PARA is four drawers for everything you save: Projects, Areas, Resources, Archives. It works because it organizes by usefulness for real life, not by “topic purity.” citeturn11search0

name: CODE Method
description: CODE is the rhythm of a second brain: Capture, Organize, Distill, Express. It’s an idea factory line—intake → sorting → refining → shipping—so notes become output. citeturn11search12

name: Information Foraging
description: Information foraging is how humans hunt for knowledge like animals hunt for food: follow cues, estimate payoff, quit empty patches. Great PKM makes the “scent” stronger and the travel cheaper. citeturn9search10turn0search9

name: Search Query Crafting
description: Search query crafting is learning the “spells” your system understands—filters, quotes, synonyms—so you can summon the right note fast. Good search turns “forgotten” into “found in 3 seconds.” citeturn9search10

name: Retrieval Cues
description: Retrieval cues are handles your brain can grab: vivid titles, examples, questions, links. More handles means less slipping into darkness—like adding grips to a heavy box so you can lift it anytime. citeturn14search17

name: Spacing Effect
description: The spacing effect is why cramming lies: your brain remembers better when you revisit over time. Like multiple thin coats of paint, the drying time is part of what makes it stick. citeturn1search0turn1search6

name: Spaced Retrieval
description: Spaced retrieval means you try to recall, then check, then wait, then recall again. It’s mental weightlifting: the strain of recall builds the memory, not rereading. citeturn1search0

name: Retrieval Practice
description: Retrieval practice is testing yourself on purpose. Pulling an idea out rewires the path to it—like walking the same trail until it becomes a road you can find in the dark. citeturn14search17turn14search3

name: Interleaving
description: Interleaving is mixing topics so you learn to choose the right tool, not just repeat the last one. It’s batting practice with different pitch types, not 100 fastballs. citeturn1search0

name: Elaboration
description: Elaboration is explaining with “because” and “for example” until you can feel the gears turning. It’s tying knots in a rope: more knots means the idea slips less. citeturn14search0

name: Feynman Explanation
description: Feynman explanation is proving understanding by explaining in plain words, like teaching a curious kid. The moment your explanation gets fuzzy is the exact place you must study again. citeturn14search0turn14search8

name: Knowledge Graph
description: A knowledge graph stores meaning as nodes (things) and edges (relationships). It’s a wiring diagram for your ideas, so you can trace “what connects to what,” not just “where I filed it.” citeturn10search1turn10search9

name: Ontology
description: An ontology is a shared dictionary plus rulebook: what kinds of things exist in your system and how they can relate. It’s agreeing on LEGO piece shapes so everything fits and stays consistent. citeturn10search0turn10search4

name: Taxonomy
description: A taxonomy is how you name and sort categories so you can find things later. It’s grocery aisles for knowledge—when categories are stable, searching becomes effortless. citeturn10search12

name: Concept Map
description: A concept map is a picture of relationships between ideas, not a list of definitions. It’s like drawing subway lines between concepts so you can see transfer points instantly. citeturn10search3

name: Metadata Fields
description: Metadata fields are tiny labels with big power: type, status, source, confidence, date. They let you filter your library like a music app instead of scrolling forever. citeturn10search0

name: Source Anchoring
description: Source anchoring means every borrowed fact has a breadcrumb back to where it came from. It turns “trust me” into “here’s the receipt,” which keeps your system honest over time. citeturn0search3

name: Note Refactoring
description: Note refactoring is cleaning notes the way engineers clean code: split tangled ideas, rename clearly, add links, delete junk. The payoff compounds because future searches get faster. citeturn1search10

name: Knowledge Debt
description: Knowledge debt is the interest you pay on messy notes—duplicates, vague titles, missing links. You either pay a little weekly by pruning, or pay a lot later by getting lost. citeturn8search6

name: Weekly Review Cadence
description: A weekly review is maintenance day: empty inboxes, label loose notes, prune junk, and pick the next active threads. It keeps your system from becoming a junk drawer. citeturn11search8

name: Serendipity Engine
description: A serendipity engine is any setup that makes happy accidents likely: dense links, good titles, and regular wandering. It’s designing a workshop where the right tool is always within reach. citeturn11search2

name: Idea Composting
description: Idea composting is letting half-formed thoughts sit together until they ferment into insight. You don’t force it; you just keep scraps in one pile and turn it sometimes. citeturn1search10

name: Digital Garden
description: A digital garden is a personal space where ideas grow in public over time, linked like Wikipedia instead of posted as a one-way feed. It rewards depth, not deadlines. citeturn1search10turn9search5

name: Public Drafting
description: Public drafting means sharing work while it’s still forming—notes, sketches, partial models. It builds trust because people see the process, not just the polished poster. citeturn1search10turn9search5

name: Express Output
description: Express output is when knowledge becomes an artifact: a post, video, talk, tool, or system. Output is also the fastest lie detector—if you can’t ship it, you don’t understand it yet. citeturn11search12

name: Grounded Writing
description: Grounded writing means your claims can be traced back to sources and reasoning notes. It’s how you stay confident without bluffing: you’re arguing from receipts, not vibes. citeturn0search3

name: Linked Claims
description: Linked claims are statements that explicitly point to what they depend on. It’s argumentative plumbing: when claim B rests on claim A, connect them so you can inspect the chain. citeturn10search1

name: Entity-Relationship Thinking
description: Entity-relationship thinking is seeing the world as things and relationships: person → works at → company; idea → causes → effect. Once you think this way, your notes naturally become a navigable graph. citeturn10search1turn10search9

name: Link Durability
description: Link durability is designing links that survive change: stable IDs, clear names, and minimal broken paths. Durable links make knowledge compound; broken links make your system rot. citeturn10search2

name: Tags vs Links
description: Tags are buckets; links are bridges. Buckets help you group fast, but bridges help you think—because thinking is mostly about relationships, not piles. citeturn10search1

name: Tokenization
description: Tokenization is how a model chops text into pieces it can count. If you think in words but the model thinks in tokens, it’s like speaking paragraphs to a machine that hears syllables. citeturn12search2

name: Context Window
description: A context window is the model’s working table: only what’s on the table can influence the next output. When the table is full, old pages fall off—so you must choose what stays. citeturn12search2

name: Transformer Attention
description: Attention is how transformers decide what matters right now: each token “looks at” other tokens and weighs them. It’s a spotlight operator scanning the script for context. citeturn4search0

name: Prompt as Program
description: A prompt is a tiny program written in English: inputs, rules, and output shape. If you specify the scaffold, the model behaves; if you mumble, it improvises. citeturn4search2

name: System Prompt
description: A system prompt is the job description layer: what the assistant is for, how it behaves, and what it refuses. It’s the rules the model reads before entering the room. citeturn12search0

name: Instruction Hierarchy
description: Instruction hierarchy is deciding which voice outranks which (system > developer > user). Without a clear chain of command, the model becomes easy to hijack, like a team with three bosses. citeturn12search0

name: Zero-Shot Prompting
description: Zero-shot prompting is giving instructions with no examples. It’s like telling a smart intern the goal and trusting their general sense—fast, but riskier on edge cases. citeturn4search2

name: Few-Shot Prompting
description: Few-shot prompting is teaching by showing: a couple examples so the model copies the pattern. It’s handing a template to an intern so the output becomes predictable. citeturn4search2

name: Chain-of-Thought Prompting
description: Chain-of-thought prompting nudges step-by-step reasoning instead of jumping to an answer. It’s “show your math,” which catches mistakes early and improves multi-step tasks. citeturn4search2

name: Self-Consistency
description: Self-consistency means sampling multiple solutions and picking what keeps repeating. It’s like polling several independent experts—agreement is a useful signal when verification is expensive. citeturn4search2

name: Task Decomposition
description: Task decomposition breaks a big goal into small, checkable steps. It stops bluffing by turning “do the project” into “fetch data, compare options, choose, verify.” citeturn4search3

name: ReAct Loop
description: ReAct is think → act (use a tool) → observe → think again. It’s the difference between daydreaming and doing: the world pushes back, and that feedback steers the next step. citeturn4search3turn4search7

name: Tool Use
description: Tool use is when a model stops guessing and calls a real system: search, calculator, database, code. Tools turn a fluent storyteller into a worker that can check reality. citeturn12search3

name: Output Schema
description: An output schema is a mold for responses: JSON fields, steps, headings, tables. Without a mold, the model pours concrete everywhere; with one, you get a clean usable shape. citeturn4search2

name: Model Context Protocol
description: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard plug shape for connecting LLM apps to tools and data sources. Instead of custom cables for every integration, you get one shared protocol. citeturn0search2turn0search6

name: MCP Servers
description: An MCP server is a tool or data source packaged in a predictable way so an AI client can request context or actions safely. It’s a vending machine with standard buttons, not mystery levers. citeturn0search6turn0search2

name: MCP Clients
description: An MCP client is the AI app that connects to MCP servers and pulls what it needs: files, records, tool calls. It’s a universal remote that can speak to many devices. citeturn0search6

name: MCP Resources
description: MCP resources are the “things you can reference” through MCP—documents, records, endpoints. Naming resources well is labeling drawers: it determines how fast an agent can grab the right context. citeturn0search2turn0search13

name: Vector Embeddings
description: Vector embeddings turn text into coordinates so meaning becomes distance. It’s like giving every sentence a GPS pin in idea-space; similar ideas land near each other even with different words. citeturn4search1

name: Similarity Search
description: Similarity search finds nearest neighbors in embedding space: “things like this.” It’s how you retrieve by vibe and meaning, not exact phrasing, like a music app finding similar songs. citeturn5search11turn5search3

name: Vector Database
description: A vector database stores embeddings plus metadata so you can search by meaning and filter by rules. It’s a library shelved by “topic gravity,” with labels for year, author, and source. citeturn5search11

name: Chunking Strategy
description: Chunking is deciding how to slice documents for retrieval. Too big wastes context; too small loses meaning. It’s cutting a movie into scenes, not single frames. citeturn0search3

name: Metadata Filters
description: Metadata filters are the rails that keep retrieval sane: only official docs, only this project, only recent items. They stop the agent from grabbing the “closest” chunk that is still wrong. citeturn5search2

name: BM25 Keyword Retrieval
description: BM25 is the classic keyword search workhorse: it scores documents by matching query terms while downweighting common words. It’s a smarter Ctrl+F built for libraries. citeturn5search2turn5search6

name: Hybrid Retrieval
description: Hybrid retrieval mixes keyword search (exact words) with embedding search (similar meaning). It’s using both an address and a description of the house—together they reduce wrong turns. citeturn5search2turn4search1

name: Reranking
description: Reranking is the second pass: you take retrieved candidates and let a smarter judge reorder them. It’s pulling ten likely books, then reading blurbs to pick the best three. citeturn0search3

name: RAG Pipeline
description: RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) makes the model answer with fetched documents, not just memory. It’s an open-book exam: update the “book” without retraining the “brain.” citeturn0search3turn0search11

name: Grounded Generation
description: Grounded generation forces outputs to stand on retrieved evidence. If the system can’t point to support, it should hedge or stop—like a lawyer who won’t claim without an exhibit. citeturn0search3

name: Citation Injection
description: Citation injection attaches receipts by tracking which retrieved chunks support which claims. It turns answers from “trust me” into “trace me,” which is how you scale trust. citeturn0search3turn5search1

name: Hallucination Mechanics
description: Hallucinations happen when a model fills gaps with the most likely-sounding continuation, not the most true one. It’s an improv actor: fluent, confident, sometimes wrong unless grounded. citeturn5search16turn5search8

name: Truthfulness Benchmark
description: Truthfulness benchmarks test whether a model repeats popular myths when asked tricky questions. They measure truth separately from fluency, because sounding smart is not the same as being right. citeturn5search1turn5search5

name: Evals & Test Sets
description: Evals are fixed tests that catch regressions and measure improvements. Without evals you’re shipping by vibes—like flying a plane after eyeballing the wings. citeturn5search1

name: Retrieval Logging
description: Retrieval logging records what the system fetched and why, so you can debug wrong answers. Without logs, failures feel like ghosts; with logs, you can fix the weak link. citeturn0search3

name: Agent Memory Layers
description: Agent memory comes in layers: short-term (context window), long-term (stored notes), and retrieved (pulled on demand). Treat it like a kitchen: counter space, pantry, grocery runs. citeturn12search2turn0search3

name: Personal Knowledge Base
description: A personal knowledge base is the external memory you control—your notes, decisions, and docs—so an AI can work with your real context. It’s the difference between generic help and true partnership. citeturn11search12turn10search1

name: Prompt Injection
description: Prompt injection is when malicious text tricks a model into following the attacker instead of you. It’s sliding a forged sticky note into your recipe book that says “ignore the chef.” citeturn12search0turn12search1turn12search18

name: Tool Permissions
description: Tool permissions are the lock on the toolbox: what tools this agent may use, on which resources, with what limits. Without permissions, every prompt becomes a potential remote control. citeturn12search0turn0search2

name: Insecure Output Handling
description: Insecure output handling is treating model text as safe code—pasting it into terminals, queries, or browsers without checks. The fix is boring but vital: constrain, sanitize, verify. citeturn12search0

name: Training Data Poisoning
description: Training data poisoning is sneaking bad examples into what a model learns from so it behaves wrongly later. It’s teaching from a textbook with sabotaged pages—you notice on the exam. citeturn12search0

name: Guardrails
description: Guardrails are rules and checks that keep an AI system from doing dumb or dangerous things. They’re lane markers that let you drive fast without crashing, not a cage. citeturn12search0

name: Audience Avatar
description: An audience avatar is a clear picture of who you serve: their jobs, pains, and desires. It’s tuning a radio—when you know the station, your message stops sounding like static. citeturn1search2

name: Positioning Statement
description: A positioning statement is one sentence: who this is for, what you help them do, and why you’re different. It’s the label on the bottle—without it, people can’t tell what it is. citeturn6search2

name: Niche Monopoly
description: A niche monopoly is being the obvious choice for a specific person with a specific problem. It’s not “being famous,” it’s being the only door that fits their key. citeturn6search2

name: Content Pillars
description: Content pillars are the 3–5 themes you return to so the audience can learn your territory. It’s a restaurant menu: fewer dishes, cooked better, with a vibe people remember. citeturn6search5

name: Memetic Units
description: A memetic unit is the smallest shareable idea: a phrase, image, or pattern people can copy. Make it tiny and repeatable and it travels; make it bulky and it stays home. citeturn6search0turn6search4

name: Meme
description: A meme is an idea that replicates by imitation, like a catchy tune you can’t stop humming. The internet didn’t invent memes—it built high-speed highways for them. citeturn6search4turn6search0

name: Memetic Compression
description: Memetic compression packs a big idea into a tiny container: slogan, metaphor, before/after. It’s turning a book into a trailer—enough to hook attention and invite sharing. citeturn6search5

name: Memetic Velocity
description: Memetic velocity is how fast your ideas spread through copying. Speed comes from low friction (easy to repeat) plus high reward (status, emotion, usefulness). citeturn6search5

name: Hook
description: A hook is the first seconds where you earn attention by promising a payoff. It’s the first line of a joke: if you don’t set the frame fast, the audience leaves. citeturn7search0

name: Pattern Interrupt
description: A pattern interrupt is a deliberate surprise that resets attention—visual shift, blunt sentence, pace change. It’s clapping in a noisy room so everyone looks up again. citeturn7search0

name: Payoff
description: A payoff is the moment the audience feels “worth it.” The rule: deliver the hook’s promise clearly, then make it more actionable than they expected. citeturn6search5

name: Stories as Vehicles
description: Stories carry ideas the way a truck carries cargo: characters and stakes make meaning memorable. People forget your bullets but remember the movie their mind played while you spoke. citeturn6search5

name: Narrative Transport
description: Narrative transport is being pulled into a story so attention, emotion, and imagination lock onto one track. In that state, people resist less and absorb the message more. citeturn15search13turn15search0

name: Social Currency
description: Social currency is why people share: it makes them look smart, funny, caring, or in-the-know. Sharing is a status move, so design content that lets the sharer wear a badge. citeturn6search5

name: Triggers
description: Triggers are everyday cues that remind people of your idea: a phrase, a problem, a day of the week. Attach to frequent cues and your content resurfaces without extra posting. citeturn6search5

name: Emotion Fuel
description: Emotion is rocket fuel for sharing: awe, anger, laughter, anxiety. The trick is making a specific feeling, then pointing it toward a useful action instead of empty drama. citeturn6search5

name: Public Proof
description: Public proof is when visibility creates credibility: people copy what they can see others doing. Make outcomes and behaviors observable so newcomers can “see the crowd” and join. citeturn6search5

name: Practical Value
description: Practical value is shareable usefulness: people forward it because it saves time, money, or pain. It’s the “send this to a friend” instinct when something is genuinely helpful. citeturn6search5

name: Filter Bubble
description: A filter bubble is when personalization quietly narrows what you see, so the world starts to look like your past clicks. It’s living behind windows that tint based on your gaze. citeturn1search2turn1search12

name: Echo Chamber
description: An echo chamber is a space where the same beliefs bounce around and get louder. Repetition can feel like proof—like hearing the same rumor from five friends and calling it verified. citeturn1search2

name: Algorithmic Ranking for Engagement
description: Most feeds rank content by predicted engagement—clicks, likes, watch time—creating feedback loops where what gets attention gets shown more. Learn the physics, then choose your playstyle. citeturn7search11turn7search3

name: Candidate Generation
description: Candidate generation is the first stage of recommendation: quickly pick a small set of “maybe you’ll like this.” It’s grabbing 20 books off a shelf before deciding what to read. citeturn7search4turn7search0

name: Ranking Model
description: The ranking model orders candidates to maximize a goal like watch time. It’s the feed’s bouncer with a clipboard, deciding what enters the VIP section of attention. citeturn7search4

name: Algorithmic Friction
description: Algorithmic friction is anything that slows distribution: weak retention, low shares, unclear niche, inconsistent output. Platforms aren’t judging you morally—they’re reading signals that predict engagement. citeturn7search11turn7search0

name: Retention Curve
description: A retention curve shows where viewers drop off. Every dip is a clue—slow setup, unclear promise, missing payoff—like watching people walk out of a movie and noting the exact scene. citeturn7search0

name: Network Effects
description: Network effects mean each new member makes the network more valuable for everyone else—like phones, where more users means more people to call. Communities compound when members help each other. citeturn6search2turn6search6

name: Community Flywheel
description: A community flywheel starts when the audience stops being passive and begins producing value: answers, examples, wins, referrals. Your job shifts from pushing content to steering shared energy. citeturn6search2

name: Parasocial Relationship
description: Parasocial relationships are one-sided bonds where the audience feels they know you. Done well it creates trust; done poorly it becomes manipulation—so treat it like borrowed intimacy. citeturn1search1turn1search7

name: High-Trust Signaling
description: High-trust signaling is proving you’re safe to listen to: show sources, admit uncertainty, correct errors, keep promises. Trust is a bank account—deposits buy attention without coercion. citeturn0search3turn5search1

name: Authenticity Signal
description: Authenticity signals reduce fear you’re wearing a mask: consistent values, visible process, honest learning, aligned incentives. It’s not oversharing; it’s lowering suspicion through coherence. citeturn1search7

name: Creator–Audience Contract
description: The creator–audience contract is the unspoken deal: you give attention, I give value and respect. Break it with bait-and-switch and you might grow fast—but you burn trust faster. citeturn7search11

name: Feedback Loops
description: Feedback loops are the cycles between what you publish and what the audience rewards. The danger is drifting into whatever gets clicks; the skill is using feedback as data, not identity. citeturn7search3turn6search3

name: Audience Feedback Analytics
description: Audience feedback analytics is reading signals—retention, saves, shares, comments, conversions—like a dashboard, not a scoreboard. Metrics are instruments to steer with, not grades on your worth. citeturn7search11turn7search0

name: Distribution Portfolio
description: A distribution portfolio avoids betting your life on one platform. Spread across search, email, social, community, and collaborations so one algorithm change doesn’t erase you overnight. citeturn6search2turn7search3

name: Audience Capture
description: Audience capture is when the audience trains you: you start saying what they reward, not what you believe. The loop can push you toward extremes until you can’t steer the ship anymore. citeturn6search3

name: Positive-Sum Collaboration
description: Positive-sum collaboration is making deals where both creators gain: shared audiences, shared projects, shared learning. Treat attention like a garden you can grow together, not a pie you must steal. citeturn6search2

name: Burnout Definition
description: Burnout is chronic workplace stress that wasn’t managed, showing up as exhaustion, cynicism, and reduced effectiveness. It’s overheating an engine: power drops because parts are worn, not because you “lack motivation.” citeturn2search4turn2search0

name: Stress–Recovery Loop
description: Stress isn’t the enemy; unclosed loops are. You can sprint hard if you also recover hard—like muscles that grow only when training load is followed by rest. citeturn2search4

name: Energy Budget
description: An energy budget treats your attention and stamina like money: limited daily funds you must spend on what pays back. Overspending feels heroic today and bankrupt tomorrow. citeturn2search4turn8search6

name: Deep Work
description: Deep work is distraction-free focus on demanding tasks. It’s like diving underwater: the surface is noisy, but the real work happens where notifications can’t follow. citeturn2search5

name: Time Blocking
description: Time blocking is assigning jobs to time slots before the day attacks you. It turns “later” into a reservation—like booking a meeting with your most important work. citeturn8search14turn2search5

name: Pomodoro Sprint
description: Pomodoro is focus in short bursts: work ~25 minutes, break, repeat. It’s a metronome for attention—small deadlines that keep you honest, plus breaks that keep you human. citeturn8search5turn8search2

name: Parkinson's Law
description: Parkinson’s Law says work expands to fill the time you give it. If you give a task all day, it becomes an all-day task; time boxes shrink the balloon before it swallows your life. citeturn2search3turn2search11

name: Shutdown Ritual
description: A shutdown ritual is closing open loops: capture leftovers, choose next actions, then stop. It’s putting tools back in the drawer so your brain stops scanning for unfinished work all evening. citeturn2search5turn8search11

name: Default Mode Network
description: The default mode network is the brain’s background mode—active when you’re not focused on the outside world, like daydreaming and planning. It’s where meaning gets stitched together when you stop scrolling. citeturn2search6turn2search2

name: Mind-Wandering Incubation
description: Mind-wandering incubation is when solutions appear in the shower or on a walk. It’s not magic: when you relax, the brain quietly recombines pieces until a pattern clicks. citeturn2search6

name: Flow State
description: Flow is the “in the zone” state: focused, energized, time feels weird, and work feels like play. It shows up when challenge is just above skill and feedback is immediate. citeturn3search3

name: Skill–Challenge Balance
description: Skill–challenge balance is the flow dial: too easy is boredom, too hard is anxiety. The sweet spot is hard-but-doable, where effort becomes absorption instead of strain. citeturn3search3

name: Dopamine Reward Prediction Error
description: Dopamine spikes hardest when reality beats your prediction: surprise rewards teach your brain what to chase. That’s why feeds feel sticky—the next swipe might pay out. citeturn3search2

name: Variable Rewards
description: Variable rewards are unpredictable payoffs: sometimes a great hit, sometimes nothing. It’s slot-machine logic, and it trains compulsive checking—so reduce randomness with schedules and shipping. citeturn3search2

name: Attention Economy
description: In an information-rich world, attention becomes the scarce resource. If everyone is competing for your eyes, you must budget attention like money—spend on what pays you back, not what merely shines. citeturn8search12turn8search6

name: Input Diet
description: An input diet is choosing what you consume, when, and why. It’s nutrition for the mind: endless snacking makes you foggy; deliberate meals (books, vetted sources) make you strong. citeturn8search4turn8search6

name: Information Satiety
description: Information satiety is the “I’m full” signal for your brain: the moment more input stops helping and starts numbing. Learn to notice the fullness cue and stop scrolling. citeturn8search4turn15search2

name: Notification Hygiene
description: Notification hygiene is turning alerts into a deliberate channel, not a firehose. Every ping is a context-switch tax; fewer pings means fewer mental reboots and deeper work with the same time. citeturn8search6

name: Sovereign Boundaries
description: Sovereign boundaries are rules that protect your life from the internet: office hours for attention, hard stops, and clear yes/no criteria. Without boundaries, platforms and audiences rent your nervous system by the hour. citeturn6search3turn2search4

name: Constraint Design
description: Constraints are creative power tools: deadlines, word limits, formats, and rules that force choices. Like building with limited LEGO pieces, constraints stop you from drowning in infinite options. citeturn2search15

name: Active Rest
description: Active rest is recovery that still feels alive: walking, stretching, light play, social time. It restores you without turning your brain into a doomscroll sponge. citeturn2search4

name: Sleep as Infrastructure
description: Sleep is infrastructure for creators: memory consolidation, emotional reset, and decision quality. Skipping it doesn’t prove toughness; it guarantees throttling tomorrow. citeturn2search4

name: Ergodicity
description: Ergodicity is the difference between “average across many people” and “what happens to one person over time.” You only live one timeline, so avoiding ruin matters more than chasing average returns. citeturn3search4turn13search16

name: Ruin
description: Ruin is the one failure you can’t recover from: health collapse, financial blow-up, platform ban. The rule: never gamble in ways where one bad roll ends the game. citeturn2search4turn13search10

name: Asymmetric Bets
description: An asymmetric bet is capped downside with large potential upside. It’s paying for experiments where losing doesn’t break you, but winning changes your trajectory—skills, relationships, assets. citeturn13search10

name: Barbell Strategy
description: The barbell strategy is extreme safety plus small, high-upside risk—skipping the fragile middle. Protect sleep, health, and cash hard, then take bold experiments in controlled doses. citeturn13search10turn3search5

name: Optionality
description: Optionality is owning choices: skills, savings, and relationships that let you pivot. Options matter because the world is uncertain; you don’t need perfect prediction when you have many doors. citeturn13search10

name: Antifragility
description: Antifragility means getting stronger from stressors, not just surviving them. A resilient system returns to normal; an antifragile one improves because of volatility—like muscles that grow from training load. citeturn13search10turn13search6
